readerTitle: Your bank says cut costs by 15%. Where do you start?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (12인 규모 철제 브래킷 제조 공장, 소프트웨어 구독 포함) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 비용 절감 목표는 수단일 뿐이다. 판단 기준은 절감률이 아니라 그 결정이 이익과 손익분기점을 어떻게 바꾸느냐다.
misconception: 비용을 목표만큼(예: 15%) 줄이면 그만큼 사업이 건강해진다. 모든 부서를 똑같이 깎는 것이 가장 공정하고 안전하다.

sources.text: 관리회계의 표준 개념 (손익분기점, 공헌이익, 고정비·변동비 구분, 고정비 배분의 함정)

factChecks.note: 맞춤 주문 라인: 매출 $30,000 − 변동비 $21,000 = $9,000. 배분 고정비 $15,000 → 보고서상 −$6,000. 셋업비 $150 × 40건 = $6,000(주문 수 유지 가정, 셋업비에는 변동비 없음으로 단순화).
영업 담당 해고: 급여 $6,000 절감, 담당 매출 $40,000 × 41.75% = $16,700 손실, 순 −$10,700. 소프트웨어 미사용 좌석 $1,500 + 유휴 지게차 리스 $2,000 = $3,500. 프레스 정지 시 일일 공헌이익 약 83,500 ÷ 20영업일 ≈ $4,175, 3일이면 약 4개월치 유지보수비($3,000/월)를 넘음.

cards.title: Your bank says: cut costs by 15%.
body: You run a 12-person plant that makes steel shelf brackets. Sales are steady. Profit is thin.
Your bank will renew your credit line if you bring a plan to cut costs by 15%. That's $27,000 a month. You have four calls to make.

image.label: Factory owner at a desk with a letter reading 15%
image.brief: 작은 금속 가공 공장 사무실. 책상 위에 큼직한 "-15%"가 적힌 은행 편지, 창밖으로 프레스 기계와 쌓인 철제 브래킷. 실제 은행 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where do you start?
body: The plant brings in $200,000 a month and spends $180,000. Profit is $20,000. The bank wants a plan in a week.

options.text: Ask every team to cut its budget by 15%
options.feedback: Fast and it feels fair. But lean teams get cut as deep as wasteful ones, and a cut to sales can lose more than it saves.

options.text: List every cost by size, and sort it: comes with each sale, or fixed
options.feedback: Slower by a day, but you see which cuts lower your break-even and which just shrink the business.

options.text: Start with the biggest fixed cost: let two workers go
options.feedback: Wages are real money. But without knowing who makes what, you may cut the people who make your best-selling brackets.

cards.title: Here's your month, sorted.
body: Break-even is $60,000 ÷ 40% = **$150,000** in sales. Notice: you can't cut 15% of your steel without making fewer brackets.

breakdown.label: Costs that come with each sale
Profit
breakdown.detail: What the bank is worried about

cards.title: A cheaper steel supplier calls.
body: Steel is your biggest cost. A new supplier offers 10% less, saving $7,000 a month. But two of their five sample batches had more rejects than usual.

options.feedback: You save $7,000 on paper. If bad brackets cost you one $20,000-a-month customer, you lose $8,000 of what's left after costs. The saving is gone.

options.text: Show the quote to your current supplier and offer a two-year contract
options.feedback: You give up some flexibility to get a lower price on steel you trust. Suppliers often move for a longer commitment.

options.text: Try the new steel on low-stress brackets for one month
options.feedback: A careful test that limits damage. But it saves little now and splits your buying power between two suppliers.

cards.title: A small cut moved your break-even.
body: That's $3,500 a month. Small, but it lands on every bracket. Each sale now leaves 41.75% instead of 40%, so break-even drops to about $144,000.

groups.label: Monthly sales needed to break even

cards.callout: Cutting a cost that comes with each sale makes every future sale worth more.

cards.title: Your report says one line loses money.
body: Small custom orders bring in $30,000 a month. Their steel and extra handling cost $21,000, so they leave $9,000.
But the accountant spreads $15,000 of rent and machine costs onto them. The report shows a $6,000 loss.

image.label: Custom order line with a red loss figure on a report
image.brief: 공장 한쪽 소량 맞춤 주문 작업대. 옆에 보고서가 떠 있고 "-$6,000"이 빨간색. 보고서 아래쪽에 작게 "Leaves $9,000"이 초록색으로 숨어 있는 느낌. 로고 없음.

options.feedback: The $9,000 they leave behind disappears, but the rent and machines stay. Profit falls by $9,000 instead of rising by $6,000.

options.text: Keep it, and add a $150 setup fee to each custom order
options.feedback: You keep the $9,000 and charge for the extra work these orders cause. Some customers may push back, so watch how many stay.

options.text: Keep it exactly as it is
options.feedback: You avoid a costly mistake. But orders that tie up your machines could be paying more.

cards.title: Now the fixed costs.
body: Say the 40 custom orders a month keep coming. The fee adds $6,000.
Three fixed-cost ideas are on your desk. Which do you take?

options.text: Let one of your two salespeople go
options.feedback: Saves $6,000 a month. Her accounts bring $40,000 in sales, which leave about $16,700 after costs. You'd be $10,700 worse off.

options.text: Cancel unused software seats and an idle forklift lease
options.feedback: That's $3,500 a month nobody will miss. The best fixed-cost cuts remove things that help no one make or sell anything.

options.text: Drop the maintenance contract on your main press
options.feedback: Saves $3,000 a month until the press breaks. A few days of stopped production can wipe out months of savings.

cards.softwareNote: In a software business, the costs that come with each sale are usually small, so most cuts land on fixed costs like people and cloud contracts. Same test: cancel what nobody uses before cutting the team that builds or sells.

cards.title: You missed the target. Profit rose 65%.
body: You cut costs by $7,000, under 4%. But profit went from $20,000 to **$33,000**, and break-even fell from $150,000 to about $130,000.
That's the plan to show the bank. It answers the real question: can you repay?

breakdown.label: Setup fee
breakdown.detail: Kept the line, priced the extra work

cards.callout: The calls that helped most were not the biggest cuts.

cards.title: Sometimes a blunt cut is the right call.
body: If cash is running out, you may need fast, broad cuts, even ones that hurt. Waiting a month for the perfect plan can cost more than a rough cut today.
And the setup fee is a bet. If custom customers leave, redo the math. Cost targets aren't wrong. They just aren't the goal. **Profit and survival** are.

cards.title: A cost target is a tool. Profit is the goal.
body: Each call used an idea from this unit:
list: **Call 1:** sort costs into those that come with each sale and fixed ones (break-even point)
**Call 2:** a cheaper input lowers break-even, but only if quality holds
**Call 3:** judge a product line by what it leaves, not by spread-out costs (product mix)
**Call 4:** cut costs that don't drive sales before costs that do (cutting costs vs growing revenue)
cards.callout: **Try it today:** list your five biggest costs. Next to each, write what you'd lose in sales if you cut it by half.
